title: The LORD's Anointed King on Zion
summary: The nations and their rulers conspire against the LORD and his Anointed One, planning to throw off their rule. God in heaven laughs at them and announces that he has installed his King on Zion. The king then reports the LORD's decree: “You are My Son; today I have become Your Father,” with the nations promised as his inheritance. The psalm ends by warning the kings of the earth to serve the LORD with fear and to kiss the Son, for all who take refuge in him are blessed.
story: Psalm 2 is the second half of the Psalter's introduction. Psalm 1 described the righteous individual rooted in God's instruction; Psalm 2 turns to the nations and to the king God has chosen. Together they set the two great themes of the book: the life of faithfulness and the reign of God through his anointed king. Behind the psalm stands God's covenant with David in 2 Samuel 7, where God promised David a descendant whose throne would last forever and said, I will be his father, and he will be my son. Book 1 of the Psalter, which begins with Psalm 3, is mostly prayers of David, and the tension between this psalm's confident king and the besieged David of the next psalm is part of the story the book tells.
historical:
Psalm 2 is a royal psalm, one of a group (including Psalms 18, 20, 21, 45, 72, 89, 101, 110, and 132) concerned with Israel's king. It has no heading, though the early church attributed it to David (Acts 4:25). Many scholars think it was composed for the coronation of a Davidic king in Jerusalem, or for its annual remembrance, during the time of the monarchy (roughly 1000 to 586 BC). In the ancient Near East, the death of one king and the accession of another was a dangerous moment. Subject peoples often rebelled, testing whether the new ruler could hold the empire together, and royal inscriptions from Assyria and elsewhere record campaigns to suppress such revolts. The psalm answers that threat with God's own decree.

After the monarchy ended in 586 BC, the psalm could no longer describe a reigning king in Jerusalem. Its placement at the head of the Psalter in the post-exilic period suggests that it was read as a promise of a future anointed king, and by the time of Jesus, some Jewish groups read it with messianic hope. The Psalms of Solomon, a Jewish writing from the first century BC, draws on its language in describing the coming son of David.
cultural:
Several images come from royal ceremony. Kings in Israel were anointed with oil at their installation (1 Samuel 16:13, 1 Kings 1:39), which is why the king is called the LORD's Anointed. The decree in verse 7 may reflect a written document given to the king at his coronation (2 Kings 11:12 mentions the testimony given to Joash when he was crowned). In the ancient Near East kings were often called sons of gods. In Egypt the pharaoh was considered divine by birth; in Israel the language was different, and the phrase today I have become your Father points to an adoption on the day of enthronement rather than physical descent.

The smashing of pottery in verse 9 would have called to mind a known practice. In Egypt, names of enemies were written on pottery bowls or figurines that were then ritually broken (the so-called execration texts), symbolically shattering the enemies' power. The kiss in verse 12 was a sign of submission and homage, as vassals kissed the feet or hand of their overlord. The call to kings to serve with fear is the language of a treaty relationship: rebels are offered terms before judgment falls.
literary: The psalm moves through four scenes of three verses each, with a change of speaker in each. Verses 1 to 3 show the nations plotting on earth, quoting their own words. Verses 4 to 6 move to heaven, where God laughs and speaks. Verses 7 to 9 give the king's own voice reporting God's decree. Verses 10 to 12 are a closing appeal, apparently from the psalmist or the king, to the rulers of the earth. The word hagah, used of the righteous meditating in Psalm 1:2, appears here in verse 1 for the peoples plotting, a deliberate contrast. The psalm ends with “Blessed are all who take refuge in Him”, echoing the “Blessed” that opens Psalm 1 and closing the introduction.

outline.t: The nations conspire against the LORD and his Anointed
God laughs and installs his King on Zion
The decree: You are my Son
A warning to the kings: serve the LORD and kiss the Son

doctrines.note: The psalm introduces the Anointed One (mashiach), the king God installs on Zion and calls his Son. It is one of the foundational texts for the hope of a Messiah, and the New Testament applies it to Jesus more than once.

God's rule is exercised through his chosen king, and the nations are promised as his inheritance. Human rebellion cannot overturn it. The psalm looks beyond Israel's borders to God's reign over the ends of the earth.
The One enthroned in heaven laughs at the plotting of the nations. Earthly powers may rage, but God's purpose stands. The psalm offers both warning to the powerful and refuge to those who trust him.

words.note: Mashiach, anointed, the source of the word Messiah (and, through Greek translation, Christ). In the Old Testament it usually refers to someone anointed with oil for an office, especially the king. Its use here for the king God installs on Zion became central to later hope for a coming anointed ruler.

Choq, decree or statute. In verse 7 the king proclaims the LORD's decree, a formal, binding declaration. The word suggests a legal document, and some think it refers to a covenant charter given at the king's coronation.

Yalad, to beget or give birth. In verse 7 God says, in effect, today I have begotten you. In context it describes the king's enthronement as a new relationship, adoption rather than physical birth. Christian theology later drew on this verse in speaking of the Son's relation to the Father, while the New Testament applies it especially to Jesus' resurrection (Acts 13:33).

Chasah, to seek refuge or take shelter. It is one of the key words of the Psalter, appearing again and again for trust in God as a safe place. The final line of Psalm 2 turns from threat to invitation: all who take refuge in him are blessed.

christ: Few psalms are quoted of Jesus in the New Testament as often as this one; only Psalm 110 rivals it among the royal psalms. The early church prayed verses 1 and 2 after Peter and John were threatened, seeing Herod, Pontius Pilate, the Gentiles, and the people of Israel as the rulers who gathered against God's Anointed (Acts 4:25-27). Paul, in Acts 13:33, applies verse 7 to Jesus' resurrection. Hebrews 1:5 and 5:5 use it to show that Jesus is greater than the angels and was appointed high priest by God. The voice from heaven at Jesus' baptism (Mark 1:11) and transfiguration echoes the psalm's words, and Revelation applies the iron scepter to the risen Christ (Revelation 19:15). The New Testament reads this royal psalm as a promise fully kept in Jesus, the Son of David and the Son of God, whose rule is not over one small kingdom but over the ends of the earth.

hard.q: What does “Kiss the Son” mean, and is it the right translation?
hard.a:
Verse 12 is one of the most debated lines in the Psalms. The word translated Son is not the usual Hebrew ben (used in verse 7) but bar, the Aramaic word for son, which also happens to be a Hebrew word meaning pure. Readers have proposed several solutions. Many, including the BSB, take it as son, arguing that an Aramaic word addressed to foreign kings is fitting and that the verse returns to the Son of verse 7. Others translate it kiss sincerely or worship in purity. Still others, noting that the Hebrew text of verses 11 and 12 is awkward, suggest a slight change that yields kiss his feet, a common gesture of submission to a king. The ancient translations differ as well.

Whatever the precise wording, the sense of the verse is clear: the kings of the earth are called to submit to the LORD and his anointed king before judgment comes. The closing line, blessed are all who take refuge in him, shows that the warning is also an invitation.

questions: The nations want to break the chains and cords of God's rule. In what ways do people still experience God's authority as bondage rather than freedom?
The One enthroned in heaven laughs at the plotting of the nations. How does that picture of God speak to your fears about the powers of this world?
The psalm ends by inviting even rebellious kings to take refuge in the Son. What does it mean for you to take refuge in him?
